opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what we believe the real bottleneck is. In embodied intelligence right now, the bottleneck is not the hardware. It's the brain: the generalization ability of the model, and the data needed to train it. So when we designed our robot, our principle was very simple: the hardware should be reliable, mass-producible, and cheap enough to deploy at scale, so that it can go out into real scenarios, work, and generate data. That's why we chose a wheeled base with two arms rather than full bipedal legs, for example.

Legged locomotion is very impressive, and it makes great videos. But if you look at what people actually need robots to do in a supermarket, a pharmacy, or a factory, most of the value is in the hands and the manipulation: picking things up, sorting, restocking shelves. Those environments are mostly flat floors. A wheeled chassis is stable, it's safe around people, it can carry a larger battery, and it can work for hours without falling over. Every extra degree of freedom you add costs money, adds failure points, and makes control and data collection harder. If the hardware is too aggressive, you spend all your energy keeping the robot alive instead of making it useful.

There's also a data argument. Our approach relies heavily on synthetic data and simulation for training, combined with a smaller amount of real data. For sim-to-real transfer to work well, you want hardware that is well understood, consistent, and easy to model accurately. A conservative, stable design lowers the sim-to-real gap. An exotic design with lots of compliance or unusual actuators is much harder to simulate faithfully.

And finally, it's about commercialization. A startup can't wait ten years for the perfect humanoid. We want robots that customers will pay for today, because deployment creates a loop: robots in the field produce feedback and data, the model gets better, and that justifies more deployment. Conservative hardware gets that loop running sooner. When the brain is truly capable, upgrading the body is the comparatively easy part. Doing it the other way around, building a beautiful body with no brain, doesn't get you very far.

r001.rationale: The response says the bottleneck is not hardware but the robot’s “brain,” specifically model generalization and training data.

r002.rationale: It discusses deploying robots at scale and commercialization, but gives no estimate of a global market of at least millions of robots unlocked by fully realizing the current hardware’s capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the core logic is actually quite simple. We're not a hardware company at heart, we're a company whose bet is on the "brain." Our real differentiation is in the model, the data pipeline, the generalization ability of the policy. If I pour most of my resources into inventing some exotic new actuator or a novel tendon-driven hand, I'm spending my scarcest resource on a problem that doesn't move the needle on what we actually care about.

The second reason is reliability. A robot that's supposed to work in a pharmacy, or in a factory, or eventually in someone's home, has to run for thousands of hours without a technician standing next to it. Every piece of unproven hardware is one more failure mode, and every failure mode poisons your data. If an arm drifts or a gripper slips in a way that isn't consistent, the model learns the wrong thing, or it learns nothing. So mature components — wheels instead of legs, proven motors, standard sensors — give you a stable platform to collect clean data on, and clean data is what the whole thing depends on.

Then there's cost and scale. We want to ship real units to real customers now, not in five years. A humanoid with legs is beautiful on stage, but legged locomotion adds enormous complexity, cost, and safety risk, and for the vast majority of indoor tasks a wheeled base does the job perfectly well. Nobody at a pharmacy cares whether the robot walks; they care whether it hands them the right box every time.

And honestly, I think there's a kind of discipline in it. It's tempting to chase the form factor that looks most like science fiction. But if you look at how other technologies matured, the winners usually took the boring, available hardware and made it do extraordinary things through software. We'd rather be the ones doing that. When the brain is good enough, upgrading the body becomes a relatively easy decision — the reverse is not true.

r001.rationale: The response says Galbot’s main bet and differentiation are in the robot’s “brain,” and argues that resources spent on novel hardware would not advance its core goals. This identifies intelligence as the current bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The response discusses shipping units and scaling, but gives no estimate of a global market of at least millions of robots unlocked by realizing the current hardware’s capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to ask where we want to take the technical risk. For us, the priority is intelligence: can the robot understand a task, handle different objects, and work reliably in an unfamiliar environment? A more complex mechanical design doesn’t automatically give you those capabilities.

Hardware still has to be capable enough for the tasks we care about. But once it meets that requirement, reliability, cost, and ease of maintenance become very important. If the hardware is constantly changing, it also becomes harder to collect consistent data and tell whether your algorithms are actually improving.

So choosing relatively conservative hardware is a way to focus our effort. We want a stable platform on which we can develop and validate the robot’s intelligence. As real applications reveal limitations in that platform, we can improve the hardware with a clear purpose.

r001.rationale: The response places the priority on robot intelligence and says more complex hardware does not automatically provide the needed capabilities, while describing hardware as sufficient for current tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not estimate a market size or say that realizing the hardware’s capabilities could unlock millions of robots.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between making impressive hardware and building a robot that can reliably do useful work. For us, the hardware is a platform for intelligence. It needs to be capable enough to perform the tasks we care about, but it also needs to be stable, affordable, and easy to maintain.

If you pursue too many new hardware designs at once, you introduce a lot of uncertainty. When a task fails, is it a mechanical issue, a control issue, or a problem with the model? A relatively mature hardware platform lets us focus on improving the robot’s ability to perceive, understand, and act.

That doesn’t mean hardware innovation isn’t important. It means we want it to be driven by actual task requirements. When we encounter a limitation that intelligence alone cannot overcome, we have a clear reason to improve the hardware. That makes the development process more focused.

r001.rationale: The response says mature hardware lets the team focus on improving perception, understanding, and action, but it does not clearly identify intelligence as the bottleneck for Galbot’s current hardware.

r002.rationale: The response gives no estimate of a global market or of millions of robots unlocked by realizing the current hardware’s capabilities.
